720	The ideal is to educate, not just to shout the truth
721	from the rooftops, the Rebbe said in a footnote. What
722	Rav Yosef says to the Tanna: my students are sitting here.
723	What do you mean? You have to come and say, there are
724	no more humble people, no rabbis, no sages. So what will they think?
725	As he said, they came to Rava: "Do not leave life for any
726	creature." If you are mediocre, will my children want
727	to be wicked? You can't. A rabbi cannot say
728	the truth about himself; he must respect himself, because
729	there are children here, students here, youths here.
730	He has to think how his words will be interpreted. This is already
731	an enormous educational lesson in itself, unrelated
732	to the essence of humility. But we want to summarize the
733	questions we asked. One: what is humility? How can one
734	grow great and remain small? What did Moshe Rabbeinu tell himself?
735	How could he stand before Pharaoh, and yet be silent before
736	his sister? That doesn't go together so well, right? The Torah
737	says to believe it, and we see that even
738	HaShem is moved by it. That means this is
739	an unnatural phenomenon; there is some depth here. Two: how
740	does humility bring strength? We said Moshe was humble, not
741	lowly; Aharon was lowly. Three: how can it be
742	that a humble man is aware of his humility? So humility
743	must be something other than what we think. And we
744	want to develop a very special point: humility
745	stems precisely from knowing your strengths, not
746	from your weaknesses. Let's say it in one
747	incredibly powerful sentence. When a person succeeds in a small way,
748	he thinks it is his own. He imagines it is thanks to
749	his talents. When a person succeeds hugely, he knows
750	it is HaShem. When a person earns 10,000
751	shekels a month, he says, well, I brought myself to where
752	I got. But when a person overtakes all his friends
753	and sees them from above, what does he do?
754	He looks at the heavens. He says: it wasn't my talents that brought me here. I have those same
755	talents as my brother and sister. How did I become
756	unique in my generation? Because they placed the crown on me.
757	Moshe's humility came from knowing that he was a figure
758	who never was and never will be like him. And so he felt
759	like a man on whom a crown was placed. He felt like
760	a courier carrying diamonds. A courier carrying diamonds
761	is not boastful. I was chosen. The mission was placed on me. All
762	I need is not to mess up. Moshe's humility
763	did not stem from weakness. It stemmed, on the contrary, from knowing
764	that HaShem chose him out of all the peoples, out of all
765	other men. And so, on one hand, it gave him
766	great firmness: HaShem stands behind me.
767	It isn't my strength. On the other hand, it gave him
768	tremendous modesty. He never felt
769	entitled to privileges. I did not create myself,
770	I did not make myself. HaShem chose
771	me precisely because He knew how great he was; he
772	understood that such greatness can only come from above.
773	It has nothing to do with me. HaShem simply
774	chose me. So what was his prayer? That I not
775	mess up, that I not ruin it, that I fulfill, that I
776	truly carry out the mission I received. What is this
777	like? Here is a lovely parable.
778	The first Admor of Gur, the Chiddushei HaRim, a student of
779	the Rebbe of Kotzk, took a small Hasidic group in a small town
780	Gora Kalwaria in Poland and turned it into an
781	enormous Hasidic court spanning the world before the war, a
782	mighty Hasidut.
783	After he passed away—he was a truly great man,
784	a huge Torah scholar of course and a great leader, but
785	materially he saw much hardship in life: of
786	13 children, I think, 12 died in his lifetime, and
787	he was left with a daughter named Esther, and a grandson remained, Yehuda
788	Leib, the Sfat Emet. The boy was 19, a youth of 19,
789	and the Hasidim choose the Sfat Emet to replace his grandfather,
790	the Chiddushei HaRim of Gur. He sits on the
791	great chair of the leadership of Gur in Poland.
792	He had Hasidim whose age was four times
793	his, who had still seen the Rebbe of Kotzk, who had still
794	received Hasidut from the great Rebbe of Kotzk. Once one
795	of the Hasidim came in to him and said: Listen, the Hasidim accepted
796	you, I accept you too, I have no complaints, but
797	do you feel comfortable? How can you, a 19-year-old boy,
798	sit on this great chair and speak to
799	people who are four times your age, who heard
800	Hasidut from the Rebbe of Kotzk and surely from the Chiddushei
801	HaRim? How do you feel comfortable speaking to them? What
802	makes you qualified for this? The Chiddushei HaRim said—sorry, said the Sfat Emet—I will tell
803	you a parable. A group of mountain climbers climbs Everest.
804	Some fell at the start, some fell in the middle, some turned back
805	midway. Two or three of the whole large group
806	managed to reach the top.
807	They reach the summit, panting, satisfied,
808	feeling they touched the heavens, and they see a small child
809	sitting at the peak playing in the sand.
810	In one moment all their illusion shattered. Look, a small child
811	does it. They say to him, how did you get
812	here? He says, "I didn't get here. I was born
813	here. I was born on the mountain." He wanted to hint to them:
814	I did not climb by my own strength. From the start Heaven
815	gave me, they chose me, they gave me the strength.
816	So it isn't my strength, it is the strength of HaShem.
817	But what does he teach them? A wise person
818	is one who does not draw the source of his strength
819	from his own ego; he draws it from the One who chose him. A wise
820	person is one who lives all the time with the feeling:
821	HaShem expects something of me. If HaShem
822	expects something of me, on one hand he stays a mensch. It is not
823	his, he is not entitled to privileges. HaShem
824	chose him, so he stays a mensch. On the other hand, this is the One
825	who gives him the strength to succeed more and more. On the
826	one hand he demands much more of himself.
827	I want to say an enormous point. I saw in the Ramban, I
828	don't remember if we once spoke about it in a class, maybe
829	yes, a few years ago.
830	It is the idea that a person should understand what his talent is, that a person
831	should understand what the talent obligates him to, that a person should understand to what
832	extent the talent is an obligation and not only a privilege. I once saw
833	an enormous point in the Ramban, about what is probably the strangest
834	story in the Torah. There is no doubt that if we look for
835	the story that seems most out of place, unrelated,
836	it is the story of Bilam's donkey. What is this
837	story? Bilam goes along the road, the donkey is pressed against
838	the wall, he strikes her, she lies down
839	under him.
